chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Salih ibn Sahl, from some of his companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

He was asked about compulsion (jabr) and pre-determination (qadar). So he said: 'There is neither compulsion nor pre-determination; but there is a station between the two, in which lies the Truth that is between the two. None knows it except the Knowledgeable One (the Imam), or one whom the Knowledgeable One has taught it.'

key_terms.الْجَبْرِ: jabr — the doctrine of absolute divine compulsion; total denial of human free will (held by the Jabriyya)
key_terms.الْعَالِمُ: the Knowledgeable One — a specific title for the Imam, the sole possessor and transmitter of this esoteric doctrinal truth
key_terms.الْقَدَرِ: qadar — here used for absolute predeterminism or the extreme of complete human autonomy (held by the Qadariyya); neither extreme is correct
key_terms.مَنْزِلَةٌ: station, intermediate position — the Shia 'middle way' (al-amr bayna al-amrayn) between jabr and qadar

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) teach about the Islamic theological debate on free will and predestination (jabr and qadar)?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) articulates the authoritative Shia doctrinal position known as 'al-amr bayna al-amrayn' (the matter between two matters): human action is neither absolutely compelled (jabr, as the Jabriyya held) nor purely self-determined (qadar, as the Qadariyya held), but occupies a middle station containing the Truth. The Imam further declares this middle truth to be a guarded esoteric knowledge accessible only to the Imam himself or to those he personally instructs, affirming the unique epistemic authority of the Imamate.
